title: AtlasBridge Dedicated decision framework — discovery
summary: Discovery call to map AtlasBridge's requirements for dedicated inference. Customer evaluating Reserved GPUs vs Hosted fallback, isolation needs for regulated workloads, expected burst patterns, and decision criteria. Agreed to run an initial 2-week pilot and share security docs + pricing tiering.
action_items: Priya: produce a sample benchmark configuration (model, batch sizes, seq-lens) and cost estimate — due 2025-07-29
Liam: send draft reserved-capacity pricing matrix and comparison vs hosted per-token cost — due 2025-07-24
Marcus: share recent traffic histogram (p95 qps, burst durations) and two sample prompts — due 2025-07-25
Sophie: request SOC2 report and network architecture for Private deployment — due 2025-07-27
next_steps: Schedule 60m pilot kickoff for the week of 2025-07-28
Redwood to propose a Dedicated pool sizing + burst credit plan
Exchange security artifacts (SOC2, encryption/KMS, SAML SSO flow)
SE to run a cost/latency tradeoff spreadsheet and share before pilot
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-22
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Liam O'Connor (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Weiss (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (CTO, AtlasBridge), Elena Torres (Platform), Marcus Li (ML Eng), Sophie Greene (Security)

[00:00] Liam: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro — im Liam, AE at Redwood, and priya and jordan are here to do the technical bits. purpose today is to understand your dedicated capacity needs so we can propose a reserved GPU plan and a fallback/hosted strategy.

[00:22] Rajiv: yeah thanks, Liam. we — AtlasBridge — are trying to decide between going hosted with bursts to dedicated reserved nodes. main drivers are cost predictability, isolation for PII-ish models, and making sure we can hit p95 latency under load. we have a regulatory audit in q4 so isolation is a hard requirement for some workloads.

[00:45] Priya: great. to start, can you give us current traffic patterns? qps, typical sequence lengths, model families? even ballparks help.

[00:58] Marcus: sure. right now in prod we run a mixed fleet — some inference on host A (cloud provider) and some on self-hosted. Typical requests are 15–60 tokens generation, small chat chains. baseline is ~40 qps steady with burst traffic up to 900 qps for 2–7 minutes during our nightly batch/ingest windows. p95 is what we care about — need < 250ms for the short prompts.

[01:35] Jordan: 900 qps burst is pretty high for that duration, ok. is that single-model traffic or multiple models?

[01:42] Marcus: mostly two models — a retrieval-augmented smaller generator plus a larger summarization model for longer flows. we can shard across models but the big one is the pain point.

[01:55] Elena: also, some tenants are regulated clients that insist on tenant-level isolation. that probably means dedicated nodes for those customers, otherwise we need strong tenant fencing.

[02:12] Priya: when you say tenant-level isolation, do you need physical isolation (dedicated GPUs) or logical isolation (networking, RBAC, encrypted KV cache)? there's a cost delta.

[02:24] Sophie: for the regulated tenants we need physical isolation or at least guarantee no multi-tenant co-residency. audit will ask for that. for others, logical isolation is acceptable.

[02:37] Liam: helpful. so we should model a hybrid: reserved dedicated pools for regulated tenants + shared dedicated for general workloads with strict fencing. question — are you evaluating Redwood Private (V P C / on-prem) for that, or is Hosted Dedicated acceptable if we can certify co-residency?

[02:55] Rajiv: we'd prefer Hosted Dedicated if the SLA and audit artifacts are sufficient — less ops for us — but we need to see the guarantees and KMS integration. if not, then Private VPC or on-prem is on the table.

[03:10] Jordan: under Redwood Dedicated we can provision reserved GPU pools (NVIDIA A10/A100 or equivalent), and you can pin model versions, set rollout policies, and configure tenant isolation. on the Private side we offer the customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM integrations.

[03:36] Marcus: what about burst handling? we can't afford 900 qps permanently. what does Redwood recommend for pre-warm, warm pools, and overflow to Hosted?

[03:48] Priya: common pattern is a base reserved pool sized for steady-state plus a warm-pool (pre-warmed nodes) for short bursts. we also provide a policy to overflow to hosted-compatible model variants — e.g., quantized versions — when the reserved pool is saturated. that keeps latency bounded and avoids queueing long tails.

[04:12] Rajiv: overflow to hosted — is that secure for regulated tenants?

[04:18] Liam: you can configure policies so regulated tenant requests never overflow. overflow is typically for non-regulated traffic. we can also reserve burst credits you pay for but only used on demand.

[04:30] Sophie: we need audit logs showing overflow decisions and full traceability. is that in the Console?

[04:36] Jordan: yes, the Console shows per-request routing, token counts, which model variant served, and end-to-end traces. there's an audit export for compliance.

[04:48] Elena: on the topic of performance: can you explain how bin packing and batching affect latency at p95? our engineers are worried that large batching to improve cost will blow up tail latency.

[05:00] Priya: right — it's a tradeoff. Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching with latency SLOs; we can cap batching time windows to avoid waiting, and we also do KV cache / prefix cache to reduce work for repeated prompts. also for long tails we recommend model quant (8-bit or 4-bit) for lower GPU memory pressure and faster kernels — but quantization can degrade quality.

[05:28] Marcus: do you have numbers for quantized vs fp16 for a T5-like summarization model?

[05:34] Priya: we can share benchmark numbers; rule-of-thumb is 20–40% throughput improvement with 8-bit on many models, but it depends. I'll include sample runs in the benchmark config.

[05:48] Rajiv: ok. another concern: networking and egress. for Private deployment we have strict VPC peering rules and need support for customer NAT and fixed outbound IPs.

[05:58] Jordan: supported. Private can sit inside your V P C with peered subnets; you manage routing. We integrate with KMS for key material and can lock down egress.

[06:10] Sophie: encryption at rest — what keys are used for model artifacts and tenant data? who rotates keys?

[06:18] Liam: for Private, keys are customer-controlled via KMS/HSM and rotations are under customer control. For Hosted Dedicated, Redwood manages keys but supports customer-managed KMS in many cases — we'll surface the exact options in the security packet.

[06:32] Rajiv: makes sense. what's the pricing model for reserved capacity? flat monthly for reserved nodes plus usage for burst?

[06:40] Liam: typical pattern is a committed monthly reservation for a pool of GPUs (sized to steady-state) with discounted rate vs on-demand. then you can configure burst credits or pay-as-you-go hosted overflow. we'll send a tiered pricing matrix: different SKUs (A10, A100) and examples of amortized cost per 1M tokens.

[06:58] Elena: can you do interpolation for partial month scaling? like we might add more reserved nodes for seasonal events.

[07:05] Jordan: yes, we have autoscaling policies and manual scaling; billing adjusts for partial months. for guaranteed capacity during events we recommend pre-booked burst reserves or temporary elevated reservations.

[07:18] Marcus: we also need guidance on A/B rollouts and canarying across model versions. if we pin versions in Dedicated, how do we roll forward without impacting latency?

[07:28] Priya: rollouts are done via the Console — you can do canary traffic to a small percentage of instances, monitor quality and latency, and then widen. Redwood can also keep a fallback policy that automatically routes back to the prior version if quality degrades or latency increases.

[07:45] Rajiv: regarding metrics, we need token-level cost breakdown by model and route, and end-user latency at p50/p95/p99. is that available?

[07:54] Jordan: yes, the Console provides token-level accounting, per-route dashboards, and traces. we can configure telemetry retention windows for your account.

[08:05] Sophie: from a security perspective, we want SAML SSO, RBAC scoped by team, and audit logs retained for 1 year. can you support that retention?

[08:14] Liam: audit retention can be extended as an add-on. SAML SSO and RBAC are supported. we'll include a sample RBAC matrix in the docs.

[08:24] Elena: for the pilot, what environment do you recommend? full Private replica or a Hosted Dedicated pilot? we want the pilot to be quick but also representative of our compliance needs.

[08:36] Priya: suggestion: run an initial Hosted Dedicated pilot that simulates the regulated tenant with strict routing rules (no overflow) so you can validate performance quickly. in parallel we can scope Private if the audit requires it. Hosted pilot shortens time to data.

[08:56] Marcus: ok that could work. for the pilot are there minimum commitments?

[09:02] Liam: pilots can be done with short-term reserved pools (2–4 weeks) and are flexible. we usually ask for a small PO for covered infrastructure, but terms can be flexible.

[09:15] Jordan: practical question — do you have telemetry with example prompts? we often see p95 blow up with certain prompt patterns.

[09:23] Marcus: yes, we'll share two prompt families and a histogram of tail durations.

[09:30] Priya: perfect. I'll take that as an input for benchmark configs. we'll run sample jobs to estimate token/sec and latency under your burst profile.

[09:40] Rajiv: one last wrinkle — some of our workloads have long context windows (3–8k tokens). do you recommend different nodes or models for that?

[09:50] Priya: long-context is heavier on memory and kv cache. we can recommend GPU SKUs and kernel selection for long context workloads. sometimes we split the request path: long-context summarization runs on larger nodes with more memory, and short interactions live on smaller, cheaper nodes.

[10:08] Liam: ok time check — we're about 10 minutes in. quick recap: we heard steady-state ~40qps, bursts to 900qps, a mix of regulated tenants that need physical isolation, desire to prefer Hosted Dedicated if security artifacts suffice, and pilot next week to validate latency/cost.

[10:28] Elena: correct. also want to be explicit about fallback — regulated tenants never overflow; non-regulated can overflow to hosted quant variants.

[10:36] Jordan: noted.

[10:42] Marcus: you mentioned quant variants — how do you characterize quality regression? do you provide eval tools?

[10:48] Priya: yes, Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regressions alerts tied to prompt sets. we can run automated evals on your sample prompts and provide delta metrics for quantized vs fp16.

[11:02] Sophie: timeline: audit in q4 means we need to be decided by end of august. what timeline would you recommend?

[11:10] Liam: recommended timeline: pilot in late July / early August, evaluate through mid-August, finalize commitment by end-August to allow procurement and onboarding before Q4. we can compress if needed but that's typical.

[11:24] Rajiv: good. procurement question — what sort of contract terms do you offer for Dedicated? SLA, maintenance windows, credits?

[11:32] Liam: enterprise contracts include SLA targets, scheduled maintenance windows, and credits for breaches. we'll surface standard SOW and SLA language in the proposal.

[11:42] Elena: any guidance on how many GPUs to reserve for our pattern? can you walk through a quick back-of-envelope?

[11:49] Priya: quick BOE: if your steady-state is 40 qps and average tokens per request is 30, that's ~1.2k tokens/sec. a single A10-ish GPU in our config, depending on model, might do X tokens/sec — we'll compute exact numbers in the benchmark. for bursts to 900 qps you either need many GPUs or rely on warm-pool + overflow. we'll size two reserved pools: one for regulated tenants sized to their steady load and one shared pool for general workload.

[12:18] Marcus: sounds good. for the pilot, can we opt-in to telemetry hooks (webhooks) so we can ingest Console events into our observability stack?

[12:25] Jordan: yes, webhooks and tracing integrations available. we'll include example config.

[12:32] Liam: ok let's close with explicit next actions. Priya will run benchmark config and return numbers; I'll send pricing and standard security packet; Marcus/Elena will share traffic histograms and sample prompts; Sophie will request SOC2 and any additional compliance asks.

[12:49] Rajiv: cool. also cc procurement once you send pricing; they'll want a ballpark TCO for the 12-month reserved option.

[12:57] Liam: will do. any other questions?

[13:02] Sophie: nothing else from security for now. thanks.

[13:07] Liam: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invite for pilot kickoff and share docs. meeting end.

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-words (V P C written with spaces, kv cache transcribed as KV cash in some segments). Some timestamps approximate.
